messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Alvarez is a 55-year-old bank teller who had spent most of her adult life trying to keep the part of herself that served in combat sealed off from the rest. During her military deployment, the moment that stayed with her was an explosion that tore through a checkpoint where her unit had been talking only seconds earlier. She remembers dropping hard to the ground, her hands scraping against a rough, gritty surface as debris and dust covered her, and hearing the kind of blast that seemed to erase all other sound for a split second before screams and shouted commands rushed in. Someone she knew did not get up. What remains most vivid is not a neat story but shards: the bang, the texture under her palms, the sight of absence where another person had been. Even now, when she tries to explain exactly what happened, she loses the thread, skips from before the blast to after it, then stops, frustrated and embarrassed. She says the memory feels so extreme that it is hard to believe it really happened to her, as if she is describing a scene she witnessed and not a life she lived.

In the years afterward, those fragments did not settle into the past. They seemed to wait for her in ordinary moments. Because the memory returned in broken sensory pieces rather than as something finished, she began to find echoes of it in more and more ordinary details around her, as if the world kept offering up scraps of the blast for her to notice. At work at the bank, if a customer starts talking about someone losing a husband, a daughter, a brother, Marisol feels her chest tighten before she has consciously followed the conversation. The rough weave of certain money bags and security pouches under her fingers can bring back the feel of the ground and debris so abruptly that she has to steady herself at the counter. A slammed door in the branch office, a dropped coin tray, any sharp bang can make her body react instantly, with her heart pounding and her muscles tensing as though she is back at the checkpoint. In those moments the memory comes not as a clear account but as disjointed flashes, and the very fact that it returns so forcefully convinces her that life is still governed by sudden catastrophe. Hearing people talk about loss leaves her with the cold certainty that everything meaningful can be taken without warning, and she finds herself thinking, again, that the world is dangerous and that there is no real safe place in it. Each reminder seems to deliver that conclusion afresh: a bang, a grief-stricken customer, the scrape of rough fabric under her hands all make it feel obvious to her that safety is temporary and that loss can come without warning.

Because the memory is so scrambled, Marisol has come to rely on vigilance more than understanding. Not being able to place the sequence of what happened makes her feel she must compensate by never letting her attention drop in the present. At the bank she studies customers’ faces, their hands, the set of their shoulders, trying to judge who may become a threat. She watches the lobby, the door, the line, the sudden movements near the counters. What frightens her most is the idea that danger arrives before there is time to make sense of it; the memory itself seems to prove that. The more unreal and fragmented it feels, the less she trusts that she would recognize danger in time unless she is on guard constantly.

That constant scanning has, in turn, narrowed her world around signs of danger. A small noise that another teller barely notices becomes, for Marisol, something to locate and classify immediately. She tracks expressions in customers for anger or volatility, and this habit keeps her attention fixed on possible threats all day. Because she is searching so hard, she notices more sounds, more sharp movements, more emotionally loaded conversations, and these become fresh triggers. By the end of a shift she is exhausted, shaky, and keyed up, having spent hours bracing for something to happen. The fact that she cannot stop scanning only deepens her belief that the world truly is unsafe and that she has to remain on guard every minute to get through it. Living with that constant sense of danger has also convinced her, more quietly but just as firmly, that something fundamental in her has changed and that she may never again be someone who can simply feel safe in ordinary life.

Over months and years this has cost her more than peace of mind. Marisol has become quieter with coworkers and impatient with customers when conversations drift toward illness, death, or bereavement, because she knows how quickly those topics can pull her under. She tries to avoid handling certain supplies when she can, passing them off casually so no one notices. She feels ashamed of how strong her physical reactions are, especially at her age, and ashamed that she still cannot tell the story straight. After one recent morning at the bank, when a metal drawer slammed just as a widowed customer was describing paperwork after her husband’s death, Marisol had to step into the break room because her hands were trembling and she could not catch her breath. What brought her to treatment was not one new event but the realization that she is living as if the explosion is always about to happen again. She says she no longer knows what in her life still feels meaningful, and she is most afraid that if she does not get help, she will spend the rest of her years guarding against danger without ever feeling truly present in her own life.
